examples: It is not hard to imagine the anxiety of the disaster victims.
It is not difficult to sense the shock that the sudden dismissal gave him.
It is not hard to understand how difficult this decision was.
The reason she won the award is not hard to imagine.
It is not hard to guess that falsifying data damages trust.
fields.explain:
Placed after an abstract noun: 想像・理解・推測・察知+ に難くない。
Often used at the end of a sentence / in the assessment part of analytical writing and reports.
Implies empathy or a rational evaluation, without expressing emotion too directly.

• Affirms that something is "not difficult" in the sense of conjecture/empathy: it is easy to imagine/understand/see.
• Not used for concrete physical actions ("not difficult to lift 50kg") → unsuitable.
• Written-language, polite nuance; often shows understanding or evaluation.
fields.notes:
• Common structure: 「N（抽象）＋は／が＋N（perception）＋に難くない」.
• Avoid it in everyday casual conversation; it can be replaced with すぐ分かる／容易に想像できる.
• Emphasizing empathy: adding 前置きに とても／大いに を is usually unnecessary, since it is already formal.
mistakes: Used for a concrete physical action → unsuitable: ×50kgを持ち上げるに難くない。
Confused with ～に違いない (strong certainty) → wrong nuance of mild inference.
Dropping the perception noun in front → awkward sentence: ×彼の気持ちはに難くない → it should be 彼の気持ちは想像に難くない。
JLPT N1: Recognize the collocation “想像/理解/察する + に難くない”.

fields.connection: N + に + N + を重ねて (same noun repeated: 苦労に苦労を)
examples: After meeting upon meeting, we finally reached an agreement.
Through experiment after experiment, we confirmed its safety.
After careful deliberation over and over, we revised the plan.
Through failure after failure, I learned my lessons.
After trial upon trial, we succeeded in optimizing it.
fields.explain:
The two nouns should be processes that can be repeated: 実験・検討・会議・調整・試行・努力・苦労.
The clause “～に～を重ねて” is usually followed by a result in the past tense or by ついに／ようやく.
Rarely used in everyday spoken language; it sounds "journalistic/academic".

• Emphasizes a process accumulated by repeating an action/procedure many times.
• Formal nuance, suited to written language, reports and argumentative essays.
• Suggests persistent effort or a chain of successive incidents (positive/negative).
fields.notes:
• N2 can be varied to avoid monotonous repetition: 協議に会議を重ねて (though this is less common).
• Combine with words indicating the outcome: ついに／ようやく／その結果／～に至った to complete the logical flow.
• In white papers/policy documents: 検討に検討を重ねて、～を策定した is a familiar formula.
mistakes: Used with a noun that cannot be repeated (× 喜びに喜びを重ねて) → choose a noun of process/action.
Missing a result after the clause makes the sentence less natural in written language.
Confused with 何度も: exams favor the formal pattern with the repeated noun.
Wrong particle: it must be “NにNを重ねて”.

examples: Depending on your exam results, you may be required to take supplementary lessons.
Depending on how the negotiations progress, we will also consider putting off the partnership.
Depending on the weather, the event will be moved indoors.
Depending on how the situation develops, the organization may be restructured.
fields.explain:
Suitable when presenting a policy or contingency plan based on objective conditions.
The second clause avoids overly subjective/enthusiastic statements; it leans toward the tone of rules and announcements.
Not used for simple everyday personal wishes (use 〜によっては in conversation instead).

• Used to state a condition that depends on the state/degree of N; the result or measure in the second clause changes accordingly.
• Formal nuance, often in announcements, regulations and minutes: “〜のいかんでは、〜もありうる/〜とする”.
• The second clause often contains a possibility, measure or ruling: 〜可能性がある／〜場合がある／〜とする／〜を検討する.
fields.notes:
• The noun before “のいかん” should be something variable/evaluable: 結果・成績・状況・答申・審査 等.
• In minutes: “〜のいかんでは、〜もありうる/〜とする/〜を認めない” is a set formula.
• “結果のいかんで” is a colloquial contracted form, less formal than “では”.
mistakes: Used with an unsuitable concrete N: ×太郎のいかんでは行きます → 太郎の都合によっては.
A command/request in the second clause sounds forced: ×結果のいかんでは、来てください → use a different structure.
Confused with “によっては”: exams often test the level of formality and the type of noun used.

examples: The tournament will go ahead regardless of the weather.
We are looking for motivated people, regardless of experience.
Regardless of the reason, applications submitted after the deadline will not be accepted.
We will publish the findings of the investigation whether it succeeds or fails.
fields.explain:
Used to declare a clear rule/policy with no exceptions.
Avoid it in casual conversation; use the ordinary “〜に関係なく/にかかわらず” instead.
Best used with an N that is common/variable (理由・天候・状況…).

• Expresses a policy/condition that does NOT change whatever N is: "regardless of / irrespective of".
• Formal tone, often found in regulations, announcements, contracts and job postings.
• Emphasizes fairness/consistency: no exceptions depending on N.
fields.notes:
• In formal documents: “理由のいかんにかかわらず、〜しない/認めない/不可とする” is a commonly used formula.
• “いかんによらず” is somewhat archaic/written, but is still found in laws and regulations.
• To emphasize "no exceptions" even more strongly, you can add “一切”: 理由のいかんにかかわらず、一切返金いたしません。
mistakes: Used with a concrete personal N → sounds forced: ×太郎のいかんにかかわらず → 太郎の都合に関係なく.
Confused with “によっては/では”: exams often test the distinction between "regardless of" and "depending on".
The second clause must state a rule/policy; avoid sentences expressing personal emotion.

examples: Depending on the weather, the event may be canceled.
Depending on the evaluation at the interview, your assignment may be changed.
Depending on the quality of the submitted work, we may ask you to resubmit it.
Depending on how the situation develops, we may need to review the plan.
fields.explain:
Often accompanies open-ended announcements: it leaves room for special cases that may arise.
It has a slight "warning/attached condition" nuance: the listener should be prepared for possible changes.
In conversation, it can be used instead of plain “によっては” to make the statement more formal and binding.

• Expresses that a result/measure may change depending on the state/degree of N; it especially implies that "an exception/special measure may arise".
• The second clause often uses: 〜場合がある／〜こともある／〜可能性がある／〜となりうる／〜も検討する.
• Common in service announcements, school regulations and business instructions.
fields.notes:
• Used a lot in business emails: “ご回答のいかんによっては、日程を再調整いたします”。
• The noun before “のいかん” should be something measurable/evaluable: 結果・状況・内容・評価・回答 等.
• “〜のいかんで” is a contracted form; “〜のいかんによっては” keeps a stronger "in some cases" nuance.
mistakes: Used with an overly concrete personal N → sounds awkward: ×太郎のいかんによっては → 太郎の状況によっては.
Confused with “にかかわらず”: one means "depending on", the other "regardless of".
Missing the "in some cases/possibly" nuance in the second clause; the JLPT often asks you to choose the appropriate clause (〜場合がある／〜可能性がある).

examples: Whatever the weather, the tournament will be held as scheduled.
Membership fees already paid will not be refunded, regardless of attendance.
Whatever the reason, lateness will not be accepted.
Regardless of the results, this project will continue into the next term.
Anyone may apply, regardless of nationality.
Whether you pass or fail, we will notify you by email.
fields.explain:
Used when the speaker wants to emphasize the consistency of a rule/policy.
More formal than ～にかかわらず／～を問わず; the range of nouns is narrower (leaning toward "situation/condition").
Not used to describe everyday personal behavior casually.
The second clause is usually an objective command/decision; rarely a personal emotion.

• Meaning: "regardless of / not depending on N", "no matter what N is like…".
• Very formal nuance, used in written language, legal documents/regulations, announcements and speeches.
• N “のいかん” = "the situation/condition of N" (如何). Not used directly with verbs/adjectives.
• The second clause is usually a decisive/general rule: ～します／～いたしません／許可しません／同様に扱います…
• Often used with category nouns: 成否（success or failure）, 合否（pass or fail）, 理由（reason）, 事情（circumstances）, 結果（result）, 天候（weather）, 出欠（attendance or absence）, 国籍（nationality）…
fields.notes:
• “如何” is originally a Sino-Japanese word meaning "how". This phrase is a set phrase in official documents.
• If the noun is too concrete (a person's name, a specific object), it is usually not used with のいかん.
• Suitable for regulations, terms and conditions, job postings and event guidelines.
mistakes: Used directly with a verb/adjective: Incorrect. It must be noun + のいかん.
Used in a casual context: Unnatural. This pattern is formal.
Confused with ～にもかかわらず (although): Completely different in meaning.
A strong personal emotion in the second clause: Unsuitable. It should be an objective decision/rule.

examples: He shouted with a face like a demon's.
The spring snow piled up like cotton.
It was a night like a dream.
She left like the wind.
The desert is as endless as the sea.
I can't leave it to the likes of him.
fields.explain:
Used when you want a formal, vivid style (literature, speeches, titles).
In everyday conversation, ～ような／～ように is preferred for naturalness.
Avoid using ごとき for the person you are talking to, as it can carry a contemptuous nuance.
Combines well with abstract nouns:夢・幻・稲妻・雷・光・神…

• Meaning: "like/as…", equivalent to ～のような／～のように but more literary and classical.
• Used for metaphors and conventional comparisons, adding imagery and formality.
• “ごとき” comes before a noun; “ごとく” comes before a verb/adjective or a whole sentence.
• Note the contemptuous nuance when used for people: N + ごとき（者） can mean "the likes of…".
fields.notes:
• Originates from “如（ごと）し” in classical Japanese; “夢のごとし” is a classical sentence-final form.
• “～するがごとく” is often seen in classical texts/speeches to create rhythm.
• When you need a neutral tone, replace it with ～ような／～ように to avoid sounding too affected.
mistakes: Used carelessly in everyday conversation → awkward style.
Confusing “ごとき” (modifies N) with “ごとく” (adverb) → wrong position.
Not recognizing the contemptuous nuance of Nごとき（者） → impolite.
Confused with ～ほど (degree) → “ごとき” is a figurative comparison, not degree.

fields.connection: [A]のやら + [B]のやら / V plain form + のやら / Na + な / Aい
examples: I can't tell at all whether he's angry or joking.
When I passed, I didn't know whether I was happy or relieved, and I was at a loss for words.
Whether it's true or a lie, nobody knows where that rumor came from.
He had a look on his face that made it hard to tell whether he was crying or laughing.
It is hard to judge whether this result is a success or a failure.
Even if I move, where on earth should I go?
fields.explain:
Used when the speaker lacks information and is uncertain; carries a nuance of confusion or mild doubt.
Often followed at the end by a verb of perception/judgment: わからない／見分けがつかない／迷う／困る.
Not used when the speaker already knows the answer; to confirm, use ～かどうか/～か.
Intonation: stress falls on のやら to show confusion.
More formal than ～のか～のか; in written language or explanations, ～のやら gives a more objective feel.

The pattern ～のやら～のやら expresses confusion/difficulty in determining between two possibilities or two states A and B ("not knowing whether it is A or B"). It is often used when the speaker only observes the outward appearance or is in a state of confusion and cannot judge clearly.
• The pair ～のやら～のやら is usually followed by a summarizing clause such as: ～か（どうか）わからない／見当がつかない／判断がつかない／困る.
• With Na-adjectives and nouns, なのやら must be used to connect to “の”.
• The nuance leans toward written language or serious expression; in everyday spoken language it can be replaced with ～のか～のか／～のかどうか.
• A and B are usually opposite or mutually exclusive, emphasizing the "unclear" nature.
fields.notes:
• With question words: 何・どこ・いつ・だれ… + のやら emphasizes "who knows…". Example: 何を考えているのやら。
• Tense/aspect: ～のやら itself has no tense; tense is expressed in the following clause (わからなかった／困っているなど).
• Avoid overusing it in casual speech if you want to sound natural: prefer ～のか／～かな when the written-language nuance is not needed.
• In literature, ～のやら can stand at the end of a sentence to create a trailing-off effect: どこへ行ったのやら。
mistakes: Forgetting “な” with Na-adjectives/N: incorrect 本当のやら → correct 本当なのやら.
Using ～やら～やら instead of ～のやら～のやら to express "not knowing": the two patterns have different functions.
Omitting the summarizing clause: many sentences need “～わからない／判断がつかない”; without it, the meaning is incomplete.
Choosing the wrong tense in the following clause: in a past context → わからなかった, not わからない.
Mixing it up with ～かどうか: when there are two specific possibilities A/B → prefer ～のやら～のやら or ～のだか～のだか.

examples: He has a tendency to put things off.
This company tends to put too much weight on short-term profits.
I have a bad habit of not listening to people until they finish.
He tends to be overly concerned with formalities.
Young people tend to be too assertive.
The department has a tendency toward inward-looking thinking.
fields.explain:
Suitable in formal writing/comments, reports and analyses.
It has a mild critical nuance; avoid using it bluntly in a way that causes offense, and add 総じて／やや to soften it.
The subject can be an individual, an organization or a social trend.

• Meaning: "have a (bad) tendency to…", "be a bit too…", "have a habit of…".
• Mild critical nuance, more formal than ～がちだ／～気味だ.
• Often used with undesirable behavior: 先延ばしにする／形式にこだわる／短絡的に考える…
• Not used for positive tendencies (praise), because “嫌い” originally means "something bad/disagreeable".
fields.notes:
• “嫌い” here is a noun meaning "a flaw/something to criticize", not "to dislike".
• Suitable when you need a gentle but weighty criticism (HR reports, performance evaluations…).
• Can be combined with 副詞: どうも／やや／少々／しばしば + V + きらいがある to adjust the degree.
mistakes: Used to praise → does not fit the meaning (because “嫌い” carries a negative nuance).
Confused with ～がちだ: “がち” is not necessarily critical, while “きらいがある” leans toward criticism.
Unsuitable subject (a specific inanimate object) → unnatural; it should be used for people/organizations/trends.
